summary: A proposal from UCSB to study how well newcomers can use the ARPANET. A group of 14 graduate students would try the computers at server sites and answer questions about user problems, site limits, where to edit files, and running cooperating processes at several sites.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC describes a UCSB study of how new users experience the ARPANET. Students tried different sites and reported problems with access, saving work, logging out and finding help.

subtitle: A UCSB study of the questions new users encounter on the ARPANET.

tldr.problem: The author asks whether a technically competent newcomer can learn to use ARPANET server sites and what difficulties might hinder that learning.
tldr.mechanism: A group of 14 graduate students used a 16-console UCSB classroom and explored network sites after introductory seminars.
tldr.outcome: The RFC lists early questions and comments from the group and says periodic reports are planned.
tldr.outcomeLabel: What the study found so far

sections.title: Questions for the Study
sections.content:
The RFC asks whether a technically competent person who knows little about network operation can become skilled at using server sites. It also asks what makes adaptation difficult and what site changes could improve usability.

Other questions concern where users should compose and edit files, how to start and control cooperating processes at several sites, and what limitations matter after a user becomes proficient.
sections.plainLanguage: The study asks whether a capable beginner can learn to use remote computers and what makes that hard. It also asks how people should manage files and programs across several sites.

sections.title: How the Test Group Worked
sections.content:
Under Professor James Howard, 14 graduate students were given access to a 16-console On-Line System classroom at UCSB, connected to the network through the UCSB Host 360-75. The consoles used keyboards with a limited key set, and the report says some protocol problems remained despite programming workarounds.

The group attended seminars, received access to local NIC files and was allowed to sign on to network systems. After an initial two-week familiarization period, students split into groups focused on different sites.
sections.plainLanguage: Fourteen students learned about the network and tried its remote systems from a UCSB classroom. After two weeks, they split into groups to study different sites.

sections.title: Early User Comments
sections.content:
Students wanted more information about accessing NCPs at different sites. They reported that UCLA-NMC was sometimes unreachable directly from UCSB but could be reached through BBN, and that results from remote Fortran or PL-1 programs could be displayed but not stored as files.

Other questions concerned confirming logout after a communication failure, contacting programmers at other sites, the best times to use each system, separate test user identifications and information about site services. The RFC says follow-up reports are planned.
sections.plainLanguage: The group found that some systems were hard to reach and that program results could not always be saved. Students also needed better information about site access, schedules and support.
